Mutations in the AARS2 gene are linked to infantile cardiomyopathy; however, the underlying molecular mechanism remains unknown. Here we report that PCBP1, a poly(rC) binding protein, interacts with the AARS2 transcript to mediate its alternative splicing. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Pcbp1 in mice impairs normal splicing and causes premature termination of Aars2, leading to defects in heart development and postnatal lethality. Similarly, mice with a deletion in Aars2 that mimics a diseasecausing splicing lesion display heart developmental abnormalities, reminiscent of those in patients with infantile mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. Mechanistically, loss of Pcbp1 or Aars2 in the heart reduces oxidative phosphorylation, a hallmark of patients with AARS2 mutations. This reduction in mitochondrial-encoded proteome activates mitonuclear communication and the unfolded protein response pathway, thereby inducing a compensatory nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene program. Our findings provide insights into the PCBP1−AARS2 regulatory axis in mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.

Congenital heart disease (CHD) remains the most common birth defect and the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in children worldwide. Although the genetics of many simple Mendelian forms of CHD have been identified, the molecular basis for most other types remains unknown. This may be due to disorders caused by multiple genes and/ or posttranscriptional/posttranslational variations. RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are key posttranscriptional regulators of RNA metabolism, controlling alternative splicing, RNA stability and translation. Although

RBPs have been implicated in heart development and maturation1–3, the roles of many RBPs remain unknown. After posttranscriptional modification, a key step in protein synthesis is the ‘charging’, or aminoacylation, of transfer RNA (tRNA) by tRNA synthetase. This process involves cytosolic and mitochondrial tRNA synthetases in separate cellular compartments, although all tRNA synthetase genes are encoded in the nucleus. Because these pathogenic variants disrupt the canonical splice donor or acceptor sites, they are predicted to cause AARS2 exon-16 skipping. We hypothesized that RBPs could interact with the AARS2 mRNA near exon-16 to help direct proper alternative splicing. We performed an in silico screen to identify RBP motif enrichment, and we found consensus PCBP1 motifs highly enriched in AARS2 pre-mRNA regions between exon-15 and exon-17 (Fig. 1a). To validate the biological significance of this observation, we performed enhanced ultraviolet crosslinking and immunoprecipitation followed by high-throughput sequencing (eCLIP−seq)19 with a PCBP1 antibody on embryonic day 16.5 (E16.5) heart tissue. We confirmed successful eCLIP immunoprecipitation of PCBP1 by western blotting and RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) (Fig. 1b,c). We mapped the location of the PCBP1− RNA interaction in the context of the transcriptome and found that 32% of Pcbp1 binding occurred within the 3′ untranslated region (UTR). In comparison, 31.43% and 23.32% were located in the coding sequence (CDS) and distal intron regions, respectively (Fig. 1d). Gene Ontology analysis of PCBP1-bound transcripts revealed enrichment of developmental processes such as ‘heart development’, ‘cell morphogenesis’, ‘tissue morphogenesis’ and ‘regulation of cellular response to stress’ (Fig. 1e). Positional motif k-mer analysis revealed that pyrimidine-rich k-mers are enriched at least five nucleotides downstream of eCLIP crosslink sites (Fig. 1f), identifying PCBP1-binding RNA motifs in the heart as pyrimidine rich with C and U repeats (Fig. 1g). Furthermore, we identified a reproducible interaction between PCBP1 and the Aars2 mRNA across the region from exon-15 to exon-16 using eCLIP (Fig. 1h). This finding was confirmed by an RIP assay (Fig. 1i). Within the Aars2 introns flanking exon-16, two regions containing CU repeat motifs that are associated with PCBP1 binding were identified, conserved between mouse and human. These regions also demonstrate PCBP1 eCLIP interaction in E16.5 heart tissue. The recessively inherited AARS2 (alanyl-tRNA synthetase 2) mutation was first described in patients with infantile cardiomyopathy associated with defects in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)5 (COXPD8, Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM): 614096). However, the knock-in mice harboring Aars2 editing domain mutations cause early embryonic lethality before heart formation6, making it challenging to study AARS2 in the context of heart development in vivo. PCBP1 belongs to the poly(rC)-binding protein (PCBP) family of RBPs; there is only one member in invertebrates but four in mammals (PCBP1, PCBP2, PCBP3 and PCBP4)7. The PCBP family plays important roles in posttranscriptional RNA processing, alternative splicing and translation regulation by interacting with pyrimidine-rich motifs in targeted RNAs8–10; they also have unconventional functions in transcription9 and iron trafficking through ferritin11–13. Germline deletion of either Pcbp1 or Pcbp2 in mice is embryonically lethal14, suggesting that they are independently essential during development. We previously generated a hypomorphic Pcbp1 mutant mouse line that exhibits abnormalities in skeletal muscle growth due to defects in the proliferation and differentiation of skeletal muscle myoblasts and satellite cells, through modulation of the microRNA processing pathway15. However, the function of PCBP1 in cardiomyocytes, especially during cardiac development, is unexplored. In the present study, we sought to determine the functional and mechanistic roles of PCBP1 and AARS2 during heart development. Using genetic and biochemical approaches, we discovered an essential role for PCBP1 in heart development by regulating the alternative splicing of Aars2, which is required for its proper function. Genetic deletion of either Pcbp1 or Aars2 in cardiomyocytes leads to a non-compaction cardiomyopathy and a significant reduction in the proteins that constitute the OXPHOS complexes, reminiscent of COXPD8 patients with infantile mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. Our findings define a previously unrecognized function for PCBP1 in regulating Aars2 alternative splicing in cardiomyocytes during development, offering insights into the RBP-regulated mechanisms underlying CHD.

Genetic deletion of Pcbp1 in cardiomyocytes leads to noncompaction cardiomyopathy and bifurcated apex formation Pcbp1 is highly expressed in the embryonic heart (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Therefore, we generated myocardial-specific deletion of Pcbp1 (Pcbp1-cKOCtnt) by crossing Pcbp1-Flox mice13,15 with Ctnt-Cre21, which depletes Pcbp1 specifically in embryonic heart cardiomyocytes (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Pcbp1-cKOCtnt appeared in expected Mendelian ratios at E12.5, E16.5 and postnatal day 1 (P1). However, Pcbp1-cKOCtnt was underrepresented at P28, indicating perinatal lethality (Extended Data Fig. 2d−h). Additionally, we found that more than 50% of Pcbp1-cKOCtnt mice died within 2 days of birth (Fig. 2a). To investigate the morphological consequences of the myocardial deletion of Pcbp1, we examined the heart at E12.5 (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j), E16.5 (Fig.2b,c) and P1 (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). The E16.5 mutant hearts exhibited a clear bifurcated apex and markedly dilated atria (Fig. 2b) and showed a thinner ventricular wall compared to control hearts (Fig. 2c). Additionally, the ventricular compact zone of the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart exhibited a reduced thickness at both E16.5 and P1 (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2r). We also observed an accumulation of blood clots in both ventricles and atria of mutant hearts, indicating impaired cardiac function (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). To analyze the heart morphology in greater detail at E12.5, we performed high-resolution episcopic microscopy of the whole embryo, followed by three-dimensional reconstruction22 to assess the ventricular morphology (Extended Data Fig. 2m−s). The Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart displayed a shorter stature with a higher width-to-height ratio (Extended Data Fig. 2o−q) and a markedly thinner compact zone in the left and right ventricles (Extended Data Fig. 2r,s). To determine cardiac function, we performed echocardiograms in neonatal mice. We found that Pcbp1-cKOCtnt pups were born with significantly lower % fractional shortening (%FS) as well as an elevated systolic left ventricular internal diameter at systole (LVID;s), with an unchanged left ventricular internal diameter at diastole (LVID;d), an unchanged left ventricular posterior wall thickness at systole (LVPW;s) and an unchanged left ventricular posterior wall thickness at diastole

(LVPW;d), suggesting ventricular dilation with systolic dysfunction without changes in ventricular wall thickness (Extended Data Fig. 2t−v and Supplementary Table 1). The cardiac function continued to decline at P1 (Extended Data Fig. 2w−y and Supplementary Table 2) and at P2 (Supplementary Table 3), with further reduction in systolic function. The progressive decline in neonatal systolic function aligns with the typical outcome of patients with left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC)23. Together, these findings suggest that PCBP1 is crucial for heart development; its deletion causes non-compaction cardiomyopathy and bifurcated apex formation.

Disrupted cardiomyocyte maturation trajectory in Pcbp1 mutant hearts To investigate molecular changes in the absence of Pcbp1, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to profile transcriptomic changes in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt E16.5 hearts. We identified 796 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), 488 upregulated and 308 downregulated, from E16.5 Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Fig. 2d). Because a delay in cardiomyocyte maturation is a hallmark of LVNC, we sought to assess the maturation state of the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart using an unbiased approach. We leveraged existing bulk RNA-seq datasets of E10.5/E11.5 (early) and E15.5/ E16.5 (late) heart ventricles from ENCODE24 and constructed gene sets that correspond to ‘Early Embryonic Heart Signature’ and ‘Late Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We then ran our Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart transcriptome against these gene sets using gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and found that Pcbp1 deficiency in the myocardium caused a positive enrichment of the ‘Early Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Fig. 2e) and a negative enrichment of the ‘Late Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Fig. 2f). These data demonstrated a clear transcriptomic shift and dysregulation in the developmental trajectory of ventricular maturation associated with Pcbp1 deficiency. To validate these findings, we performed in situ hybridization to label chamber maturation-related transcripts in E16.5 hearts. We found that the expression of Myl4, Myl7 (Fig. 2g) and Bmp10 (Fig. 2h) mRNAs was restricted to the atrium in the wild-type control E16.5 heart, consistent with previous studies25,26. However, ectopic expression of these mRNAs was found in the myocardium and trabecular zones of Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Fig. 2g,h). These results suggest that Pcbp1 deficiency results in ventricular developmental delay. PCBP1 regulates alternative splicing events and exon skipping of Aars2 in the heart To investigate whether PCBP1 regulates alternative splicing in cardiomyocytes, we performed alternative splicing analysis and identified 542 alternatively spliced genes from Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts. These alternatively spliced genes can be classified into five major classes of splicing events: alternative 3′ splice site, alternative 5′ splice site, skipped exon, retained intron and mutually exclusive exon (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 4a). We identified 341 skipped exon events, accounting for 62.92% of the total detected alternatively spliced events in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Fig. 2i,j). Additionally, we found 84 retained intron events, which comprise 15.5% of the alternatively spliced events, and the rest of the categories account for less than 8% each (Extended Data Fig. 4b,d−g). Notably, the alternatively spliced events that we identified in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts showed minimal overlap with those found in HepG2 or K562 cells after PCBP1 small interfering RNA (siRNA) treatment, suggesting that alternative splicing is most likely regulated in a cell-type-specific manner (Extended Data Fig. 4c). We next asked whether alterations in the skipped exon pattern in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts are directly associated with PCBP1 binding. We generated an RNA map of PCBP1-bound mRNA transcripts corresponding to the pattern of their alternatively spliced events in control and Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts at E16.5 (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 4h−l). PCBP1 eCLIP peaks located at the 5′ and 3′ flanking intronic regions of all alternatively spliced cassette exons were enriched only in the skipped exon loci from the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts. (Fig. 2k, top, and Extended Data Fig. 4h). However, a similar enrichment was not observed for the exon inclusion events or any of the less frequently observed alternatively spliced categories (Fig.2k, bottom, and Extended Data Fig. 4i−l). These data suggest that Pcbp1 may regulate exon skipping to stabilize target transcripts in the developing heart. To better understand the molecular mechanism underlying PCBP1-mediated exon skipping and to identify its regulatory targets, we focused on genes that exhibit skipped exon in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts and that show PCBP1 binding at their 5′ or 3′ splice sites; these analyses identified 34 genes with both features (Fig. 2l). We found that Aars2 exon-16 junction usage was dramatically decreased in the absence of Pcbp1

in both E16.5 and E12.5 hearts (Fig. 2m and Extended Data Fig. 5a−h). This alternative splicing regulation by PCBP1 is cell autonomous, as we observed similar exon skipping in HL-1 cells with Pcbp1 knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 5i−k). Consistent with our previous mapping of PCBP1 binding sites near AARS2 exon-16, loss of Pcbp1 resulted in significant skipping of Aars2 exon-16, supporting a direct role for PCBP1 in regulating this splicing event. Skipping Aars2 exon-16 results in a downstream frameshift, producing premature termination signals (Extended Data Fig. 5l), which likely affect transcript stability and protein translation. Consistent with this prediction, the mRNA level of Aars2, measured by detecting the region spanning exon-14 to exon-15, a common region in all transcript variants, was reduced by 46% and 59%, respectively, at E12.5 and E16.5 in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Extended Data Fig. 5m,n). Similarly, the amount of AARS2 protein in the E16.5 Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts was dramatically reduced to only 13.7% of the control level (Fig. 2n−p). These findings indicate a robust regulatory role for PCBP1 in Aars2 exon-16 skipping and in controlling AARS2 protein levels in the developing heart.

PCBP1 and AARS2 regulate integrated stress response and OXPHOS in embryonic hearts We found unfolded protein response (UPR) as the top upregulated pathway in hearts of Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt mice. GSEA showed that both had significantly increased UPR-related gene expression (Fig. 4a,b). The UPR is a highly conserved protein quality control system that is activated when cells have impaired folding of nascent proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum30 or in the mitochondria during mitochondrial dysfunction31. Mitochondrial dysfunction also induces the integrated stress response (ISR), a branch of UPR mediated by ATF4 (refs. 32–39). UPR/ISR targets such as Ddit3, amino acid nutrient stress gene Asns40 as well as Atf4 were also elevated in both Pcbp1-cKOCtnt (Fig. 4c−e,i) and Aars2-cKOCtnt (Fig. 4f−h,k) hearts. Furthermore, the protein level of ATF4 and Ser51 p-eIF2α was about twice as high in both Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt hearts at E16.5 (Fig. 4j,l). Because p-eIF2α can be activated by both ISR and UPR, we sought to characterize other UPR arms independent of eIF2α phosphorylation. Upon UPR activation, endoplasmic reticulum-bound ATF6 is cleaved to produce a nuclear form (ATF6-N), which contains the bZIP DNA binding and transactivation domains, and act as a potent transcription factor41,42. We assayed ATF6-N levels by western blotting and found that it was elevated in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt embryonic hearts at E16.5 but not in Aars2-cKOCtnt hearts (Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). We examined endoplasmic

reticulum chaperone GRP78 (BiP), XBP1-s, HSP60 and phosphorylation of IRE1, GCN2 and PERK in E16.5 hearts but found no protein-level differences in either Pcbp1-cKOCtnt or Aars2-cKOCtnt embryonic hearts (Extended Data Fig. 7a−d). However, LONP1, the main protease in the mitochondrial matrix that degrades damaged proteins, was elevated in Aars2-cKOCtnt but not in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). The differences in the UPR/ISR response between Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt embryonic hearts, particularly in ATF6 and LONP1, may explain the difference in severity of their phenotypes. Our data show that the eIF2α-ATF4 arm of the UPR/ISR is consistently activated when either Pcbp1 or Aars2 is deleted in the myocardium. We also saw an overall increase in aminoacyl-tRNA transferase (ARS) in both Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt hearts (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f), with 11 cytosolic ARS transcripts upregulated in both models (Extended Data Fig. 7g). Cytosolic ARS activation, linked to stress response, was previously associated with transcriptional activation via ATF4 (ref. 43). These findings indicate that loss of Pcbp1−Aars2 results in a unified shift in the UPR/ISR stress response in both models. By P28, %FS declined with further dilation and wall changes, suggesting reduced systolic function. Dilation worsened by P42, with %FS dropping to 7.10 ± 3.80 compared to controls (approximately 42.9), indicating severe heart failure (Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Tables 4−8). Consistent with these findings, we observed severe cardiac dilation and ventricular wall thinning via hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Fig. 6f, top), along with cardiac fibrosis detected by Sirius Red/Fast Green staining at P56 (Fig. 6f, bottom). Transmission electron microscopy at P21 shows a decrease in mitochondrial cristae density in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, whereas sarcomere structure remains normal in both Aars2-cKOMyh6 and control animals (Fig. 6g, top, and Fig. 6h). These observations demonstrate that Aars2-cKOMyh6 animals develop a progressive dilated cardiomyopathy, marked by diminished cardiac contractility and severe heart failure in later stages, likely contributing to the postnatal lethality. under denaturing conditions, where the catalytic core and protein components of C-I, C-III and C-IV were compromised at the protein level, as shown in both whole-heart lysates and isolated mitochondria (Fig. 6m and Extended Data Fig. 8t−w). Interestingly, no reduction in protein level was detected for the components of C-II (SDHB) and C-V (vATP5A). To test this, we examined P21 and P42 samples for the expression of key components of UPR/ISR. We observed activation of PERK and GCN2 via phosphorylation at P21 (Extended Data Fig. 9a). These two proteins are key sensors of the ISR, with PERK also involved in the UPR33. In the mutant hearts at P21, levels of p-eIF2α, ATF4 and ASNS were increased, and they rose further at P42, along with the upregulation of LONP1, a downstream target of ATF4 (Fig. 6n and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Moreover, UPR target genes endoplasmic reticulum chaperone GRP78 (BiP), phosphatase GADD34, ATF6-N and CHOP were elevated in the Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts at P21 (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Our data show that loss of Aars2 activates both UPR and ISR responses, with sustained eIF2α phosphorylation. A human COXPD8 sample with AARS2 mutations45 also showed increased eIF2α phosphorylation, ASNS and LONP1 (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f). Additionally, AARS2 protein levels in the human COXPD8 patient’s heart were lower than in normal samples (Extended Data Fig. 9d), aligning with previous findings that mutations in the AARS2 editing domain cause protein instability17. Loss of Aars2 in the heart results in the activation of the nuclear-encoded mitochondrial translation program and mitonuclear communication To understand the molecular mechanisms of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy caused by Aars2 deficiency, we performed RNA-seq and tandem mass tag (TMT) proteomics on P14 and P21 Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts (Fig. 7a and Extended Data Fig. 10a,b). We integrated transcriptomic and proteomic results at both timepoints. At P14, 234 genes changed only in transcript levels, 314 only in protein levels and 33 in both (Extended Data Fig. 10c). At P21, more genes showed differences, especially in transcriptome analysis: 1,402 in transcript levels, 525 in protein levels and 333 in both (Fig. 7a). Most genes regulated by both RNA and protein at either timepoint were concordant with linear RNA−protein relationships (Fig. 7b and Extended Data Fig. 10d). Aars2, from which exon-16 was conditionally deleted, was significantly reduced at RNA and protein levels at both times (Fig. 7b and Extended Data Fig. 10d). Mitochondrial-encoded proteins were substantially reduced in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, consistent with the role of Aars2 in mitochondrial translation (Fig. 7c). Protein-only downregulated genes were overrepresented in mitochondrial respiratory chain/OXPHOS pathways, indicating an overall translational defect of OXPHOS complexes (Extended Data Fig. 10e,f). Because mitochondrial translation must be coordinated for proper assembly of the OXPHOS system46, the overall reduction in mitochondrial-encoded proteins observed in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts aligns with the OXPHOS defects seen in both Aars2-cKOCtnt and Pcbp1-cKOCtnt embryos. Conversely, genes that are upregulated in both RNA and protein levels in P21 Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, such as MTHFD2, PHGDH, ASNS, SLC7A5, PYCRL, PSAT1 and LONP1, are known to be activated by the mitochondrial UPR/ISR pathway. This supports our conclusion that PCBP1 and AARS2 are key regulators of the stress response. Additionally, in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, five mitochondrial-encoded proteins (MT-ND2, MT-ND5, MT-CO1, MT-CO2 and MT-CO3) are discordantly regulated, with increased transcripts but decreased protein levels (Fig. 7b). These results suggest that mitochondrial translation defects may trigger a compensatory response, leading to transcriptional activation of these genes. Discussion Mutations of the Aars2 gene, including those that affect its splicing, are linked to human congenital mitochondrial cardiomyopathy5,53. In the present study, we generated mouse models to demonstrate that cardiomyocyte-specific Aars2 mutations cause cardiac defects in embryonic and postnatal hearts, mimicking those observed in patients. Our studies implicate PCBP1, an RBP that directly interacts with Aars2 RNA to regulate its splicing, as a crucial molecule required for proper AARS2 function; furthermore, genetic deletion of Pcbp1 in cardiomyocytes phenocopies cardiac defects found in Aars2 mutant mice. We found that loss of PCBP1−AARS2 in cardiomyocytes reduces mitochondrial and OXPHOS function. Pcbp1 and Aars2 mutant mice also exhibit an activation of the UPR/ISR pathway and enhanced mitonuclear communication. Our study highlights an important role for PCBP1 in cardiac development and function by regulating Aars2 exon-16 inclusion, providing a molecular explanation for how Aars2 mutations cause infantile mitochondrial cardiomyopathy (Fig. 8). Mechanistically, we found that PCBP1 plays a pivotal role in regulating Aars2 alternative splicing and gene expression in cardiomyocytes during heart development. We and others previously found that germline knockout of Pcbp1 causes preimplantation lethality before heart formation, indicating its role during gastrulation14,15. A nonsense variant of human PCBP1, c.550 C > T, is likely pathogenic, with clinical features including developmental delay, short stature, Tetralogy of Fallot and decreased muscle mass54. These support a

role for PCBP1 in heart development and link mutations to congenital heart defects. Cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pcbp1 resulted in perinatal lethality, non-compaction cardiomyopathy and defects in ventricular apex formation, underscoring the essential role of Pcbp1 in cardiac development. Our study reveals the role of PCBP1 in RNA splicing, specifically its regulation of Aars2 alternative splicing in the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart, in which exon-16 is skipped. Our eCLIP−seq, RIP and minigene experiments support the conclusion that PCBP1 stabilizes this splicing by binding to mRNA. Loss of Pcbp1 causes Aars2 exon-16 skipping, and mutation of PCBP1 motifs flanking Aars2 exon-16 also leads to skipping. Therefore, PCBP1 likely acts as a splicing modulator55, with future work aimed at identifying other ribonucleoprotein complexes involved. AARS2-related infantile cardiomyopathy involves a recurrent pathogenic p.Arg592Trp mutation in the editing domain, found in homozygous or compound heterozygous patients17. Data from modeling the human AARS2 p.Arg592Trp and p.Arg580Trp mutations suggest that these mutations cause a reduction of AARS2 protein and are sufficient to cause a severe defect in mitochondrial protein synthesis. Additional AARS2 damaging mutations have recently been reported in the intronic splice donor site (c.2255+1 G > A) and acceptor site (c.2146-2 A > G) flanking exon-16 of the AARS2 gene56,57, and our experimental data suggest that such mutations cause AARS2 mRNA mis-splicing and loss of function. We speculate that our loss-of-function Aars2 mouse models, which also display mitochondrial translation defects, share a similar pathological mechanism with the human disease. Our Aars2-cKOCtnt mice are embryonically lethal and exhibit LVNC, as do Pcbp1-cKOCtnt mice. Both display OXPHOS deficiency, indicating that they are in the same regulatory axis, linking AARS2-related infantile cardiomyopathy to exon-16 splicing in patients. Aars2-cKOCtnt has a more severe phenotype, likely due to earlier Aars2 deficiency (Cre recombination), compared to Pcbp1-cKOCtnt, where Pcbp1 deletion and Aars2 mis-splicing take longer and require more steps. Furthermore, there may be additional PCBP1-dependent, AARS2-independent pathways that oppose the damaging effects from Aars2 depletion. From late gestation, more than half of the ATP generated in the heart relies on OXPHOS, and this balance shifts toward further reliance on OXPHOS after birth58, which is essential for postnatal cardiomyocyte development and maturation59. Direct perturbation of OXPHOS in the embryonic heart can lead to severe heart defects and lethality60–62. The results of our genetic approach to delete the Aars2 gene in embryonic and postnatal mouse hearts confirm its function in heart development and cardiomyopathy. We also found that destabilization of C-I and C-IV occurred in Aars2-cKOMyh6 mice before the onset of cardiomyopathy, indicating that the assembly and turnover of C-I and C-IV are more sensitive to mitochondrial translational defects caused by Aars2 deficiency and are likely the primary causes of the mitochondrial catastrophe that follows. Our finding is consistent with the notion that the turnover of unassembled OXPHOS subunits occurs primarily at the protein level via mitochondrial proteases63,64, and the precise mechanism underlying the selective sensitivity warrants further exploration. We identified MYC as a key transcription factor activated by Aars2 loss of function, promoting mitochondrial and ribosomal biogenesis. Because AARS2 regulates mitochondrial translation, the observed defects and nuclear activation of the UPR/ISR and MYC programs are likely linked as part of retrograde mitonuclear communication in response to cellular stress. Interestingly, MYC can upregulate ATF4 by activating GCN2 via uncharged tRNAs, and ATF4 and MYC co-occupy the promoter of some MYC targets, regulating amino acid and protein synthesis65. It remains to be seen if this transcriptional crosstalk occurred similarly in mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. Our data show that the PCBP1−AARS2 axis induces UPR/ISR, possibly by disrupting mitotranslation, and activates MYC and ATF4. Further studies are needed to identify the downstream targets and pathways regulated by this axis in cardiac development and CHD. Our findings reveal how the RBP PCBP1 regulates splicing of the mitochondrial tRNA aminoacyl transferase AARS2, which is linked to mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. The PCBP1−AARS2 axis safeguards mitochondrial translation and stabilizes OXPHOS complexes in the heart. Given the lack of effective treatments for OXPHOS deficiency diseases, our study advances understanding of the tissue-specific regulatory mechanisms involved and may identify potential therapeutic targets.

Methods All murine experiments were performed in accordance with approved protocols of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Boston Children’s Hospital and the University of Southern California. Animal husbandry and gene manipulations CRISPR−Cas9 pronuclear microinjection was used to generate Aars2-Flox and deletion mutant mice at the Mouse Gene Manipulation Core of Boston Children’s Hospital as previously described66 with minor modifications. In brief, a cocktail of 0.61 pmol µl−1 each of crRNA+tracrRNA, 100 ng µl−1 Cas9 protein and 10 ng µl−1 ssODN (Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)) or ds-Donor DNA was injected into the pronuclei of E0.5 embryos (C57BL6/Harlan). Surviving embryos were reimplanted into recipient CD1 pseudo-pregnant females and allowed to develop to term. The resultant pups were genotyped by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and genome-edited founders were identified and verified by TOPO cloning followed by Sanger sequencing. Two founders were chosen from each line and backcrossed to C57BL/6 (Harlan) for three generations to establish lines. Genotyping primers for screening founders are listed in Supplementary Table 9.

We obtained a Pcbp1-Flox allele13 for conditional knockout generation. Mice carrying Pcbp1-Flox or Aars2-Flox were bred with Tg(Tnnt2-cre)5Blh/JiaoJ (Ctnt-Cre)21 or Tg(Myh6-cre)2182Mds/J44 to generate corresponding cardiac-specific conditional deletions (Pcbp1-cKOCtnt, Aars2-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOMyh6). All data presented here for Pcbp1-cKOCtnt are from the previously described nonhypomorphic Pcbp1-Flox allele13, although we also examined our independently generated hypomorphic Pcbp1-Flox allele15 for conditional knockout and observed a very similar phenotype. All animals were maintained on a 12-hour light cycle, at specific pathogen-free facilities. Genetically modified strains of mice were genotyped by isolating genomic DNA from a tail tip excision and subjecting the DNA to PCR using primers corresponding to the modification. For timed pregnancy experiments, 2-month-old males and females from indicated lines and genotypes were co-housed, and the vaginal plugs of the female mice were checked each morning after the date of co-housing to approximate the date of gestation, with the day of vaginal plug appearance noted as E0.5. Mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation according to approved protocols.

Human tissue Heart tissue from a single COXPD8 patient (diagnosed premortem) and three unrelated comparison patients, who died from various causes between 1 day and 5 months of life, were authorized for research and provided, with deidentified clinical data, through the Developmental Lung Molecular Atlas Program (LungMAP) Human Tissue Core and BioRepository for Investigation of Neonatal Disease of the Lung (https://brindl.urmc.rochester.edu/labkey/home/project-begin.view), managed by Gloria Pryhuber (University of Rochester). Deidentified clinical metadata and next-of-kin authorizations for each heart sample used in research were provided by the Organ Procurement Organizations. Aliquots of heart samples were harvested and frozen at −80 °C for experimental use. Details are presented in Beutner et al45.

Differentiation of hiPSC-CMs hiPSC-CMs were generated using the STEMdiff Ventricular Cardiomyocyte Differentiation Kit (STEMCELL Technologies, 05010) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. eCLIP−seq eCLIP studies were performed according to the published single-end enhanced CLIP (seCLIP) protocol76 with the following modifications (Eclipse Bioinnovations). Approximately 80 mg of frozen embryonic mouse heart tissue was cryogrinded and ultraviolet crosslinked at 400 mJoules cm−2 with 254-nm radiation. The equivalence of 75 μg of RNA was lysed using 1 ml of eCLIP lysis mix and subjected to two rounds of sonication for 4 minutes with 30 seconds ON/OFF at 75% amplitude. A prevalidated PCBP1 antibody (Abcam, ab168377) was then precoupled to anti-rabbit IgG Dynabeads (Thermo Fisher Scientific), added to the lysate and incubated overnight at 4 °C. Before immunoprecipitation, 2% of the sample was taken as the paired input sample, with the remainder magnetically separated and washed with eCLIP high-stringency wash buffers. Immunoprecipitation and input samples were cut from the membrane at the relative band size of 40−75 kDa above that band size. RNA adapter ligation, immunoprecipitation− western blot, reverse transcription, DNA adapter ligation and PCR amplification were performed as previously described19. The eCLIP cDNA adapter contains a sequence of 10 random nucleotides at the 5′ end. This random sequence serves as a unique molecular identifier (UMI) after sequencing primers are ligated to the 3′ end of cDNA molecules77. Therefore, eCLIP reads begin with the UMI, and, in the first step of analysis, UMIs were pruned from read sequences using umi_tools (version 0.5.1)78. UMI sequences were saved by incorporating them into the read names in the FASTQ files to be used in subsequent analysis steps. Next, 3′ adapters were trimmed from reads using Cutadapt (version 2.7)79, and reads shorter than 18 bp were removed. Reads were then mapped to a database of human and mouse repetitive elements, and rRNA sequences were compiled from Dfam80 and GenBank81. All non-repeat mapped reads were mapped to the mouse genome (mm10) using STAR (version 2.6.0c)82. PCR duplicates were removed using umi_tools (version 0.5.1) by using UMI sequences from the read names and mapping positions. Peaks were identified within eCLIP samples using the peak caller CLIPper (https:// github.com/YeoLab/clipper)83, using parameters consistent with ENCODE standards. For each peak, immunoprecipitation versus input fold enrichment values were calculated as a ratio of counts of reads overlapping the peak region in the immunoprecipitation and the input samples (read counts in each sample were normalized against the total number of reads in the sample after PCR duplicate removal). A P value was calculated for each peak by Yates’ χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test if the observed or expected read number was lower than 5. Comparison of different sample conditions was evaluated in the same manner as immunoprecipitation versus input enrichment; for each peak called in immunoprecipitation libraries of one sample type, we calculated enrichment and P values relative to normalized counts of reads overlapping these peaks in another sample type. Peaks were annotated using transcript information from GENCODE84 with the following

priority hierarchy to define the final annotation of overlapping features: protein-coding transcripts (CDS, UTR and intron), followed by non-coding transcripts (exon and intron). De novo motif discovery for peaks detected was performed using HOMER (version 4.11), and the positionally enriched k-mer analysis (PEKA) in whole gene, 3′ UTR, intron or exon regions was performed using PEKA software (https:// github.com/ulelab/peka)85.

Proteomic sample preparation and liquid chromatography− tandem mass spectrometry analysis Mice were euthanized and subjected to transcardial perfusion with PBS. Hearts were dissected, snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. To perform the protein extraction, hearts were ground over liquid nitrogen and resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 100 mM NaCl and 0.5 mM EDTA) supplemented with protease inhibitor and phosphatase inhibitors 2 and 3 (Sigma-Aldrich). Samples were subjected to dounce homogenization for 20 strokes and resuspended in SDS buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 100 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 2% SDS and inhibitors). Subsequently, samples were heated at 95 °C for 5 minutes, followed by sonication. Heating and sonication steps were repeated three times. Samples were centrifuged at 2,000g for 5 minutes at room temperature to remove insoluble debris. Protein concentrations were determined by BCA assay. One hundred micrograms of protein was reduced and alkylated with 25 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine and 50 mM chloroacetamide, respectively, for 20 minutes at 70 °C. Samples were then precipitated using a methanol/chloroform protocol. Protein pellets were snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Three biological replicates were collected for each age/sex. Protein pellets were reconstituted with 1 M urea in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol at 56 °C for 30 minutes and then alkylated with 15 mM iodoacetamide at room temperature in the dark for 45 minutes. The samples were subjected to digestion with LysC (Wako) for 2 hours and trypsin (Promega) overnight at 37 °C. Peptide samples were cleaned using Pierce Desalting Spin Columns, and then peptide quantitation was conducted using the Pierce fluorometric peptide BCA assay. Twenty micrograms of each sample was aliquoted and dried down for TMT labeling. Samples were divided into two sets by age (P14 and P21). Three pooled samples were created to assess technical reproducibility and assess batch effects from the two sets. Additionally, these pooled samples could be used to bridge the TMT datasets. Each sample was labeled using TMTpro 16-plex reagents. After confirming ideal labeling efficiency, the TMT-labeled samples were quenched, combined and cleaned using Pierce Desalting Spin Columns. Samples were mixed (multiplexed) and subjected to off-line high-performance liquid chromatography fractionation (high-pH reversed-phase). Fractions were combined down to a total of 24 fractions per TMT set. Each fraction was analyzed by liquid chromatography−tandem mass spectrometry (LC−MS/MS) using an UltiMate 3000-Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Proteins were identified and quantified with Proteome Discoverer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, version 2.5) using a UniProt mouse database (approximately 17,000 proteins), appended with a common contaminants database. Data were normalized, and missing values were imputed. Proteome-level filtering: 1% peptide/5% protein FDR, minimum of two peptides, proteins quantified in a minimum of 50% of samples. Further data analysis, including statistical analysis and visualization, was conducted within Proteome Discoverer. For analyzing the mitochondrial protein within the proteome, we used Mouse MitoCarta3.0 (ref. 87), an inventory of experimentally supported mitochondrial localizing proteins. We used the heart-expressing subset of mitochondrial-localized proteins (nuclear encoded and mitochondrial encoded) within the MitoCarta3.0 database to subset our proteomics datasets for mitoproteins.

then aligned to the mouse genome (mm10, obtained from the UCSC Genome Browser) using Bowtie 2. SAM files from Bowtie 2 alignment were subsequently input into HOMER to perform peak calling across biological replicates using getDifferentialPeaksReplicates.pl. The return peaks that have at least two-fold enrichment with FDR < 0.05, located at (−2,000, +500), were considered peaks near the promoter. Principal component analysis and enrichment analysis We defined expressed genes as those that have expression in at least half of all samples. Expressed genes were subjected to principal component analysis (PCA); unit variance scaling was applied to rows; and singular value decomposition with imputation was used to calculate principal components. Principal components 1 and 2 were plotted in two-dimensional coordinates. GSEA was performed on expressed genes according to the software manual88. Gene sets with nominal P < 0.05 and FDR < 0.25 were considered significant. All expressed genes were log2 transformed and centered, and unsupervised hierarchical clustering and visualization were performed with ClustVis89. Gene Ontology enrichment analysis was performed using either the R package clusterProfiler90 with enrichGO and the compareCluster function or ShinyGO (0.80)91. For identifying putative upstream transcription factors, we performed the analysis with the ENCODE_and_ ChEA_Consensus_TFs_from_ChIP-X library from Enrichr92, which is a database containing genes where transcription factor binds in the vicinity of their promoter regions. Gene regulatory network analysis was performed with Metascape93. In brief, all protein−protein interactions (PPIs) among input genes were extracted from an integrated PPI data source (STRING, BioGrid, OmniPath and InWeb_DB) and formed a PPI network. The MCODE algorithm was then applied to this network to identify neighborhoods where proteins are densely connected. Each MCODE network is assigned with a unique color, and Gene Ontology enrichment analysis was applied to each MCODE network to extract biological meaning, where the top three best P value terms were retained.

Statistics Values are reported as means ± s.e.m. unless indicated otherwise. A one-way ANOVA, followed by Tukeyʼs post hoc testing, was used to evaluate the statistical significance of multiple-group comparisons. In addition, the two-tailed non-parametric Student’s t-test was used for two-group comparisons. Values of P < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
